query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor additive that promotes in-situ nanoprecipitate formation within the CoCrFeNi matrix will enable the development of a nanohierarchical microstructure that adaptively protects the friction interface across the sliding temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional single-phase, coarse-grained CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Alloying the base CoCrFeNi with a small amount of a nanoprecipitate‐forming element (e.g., titanium) during processing to induce a distribution of stable, fine nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests conducted in ambient air under controlled loads at temperatures ranging continuously from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanohierarchical microstructure featuring a matrix of ultra-fine grains coupled with dispersed, coherent nanoprecipitates.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the nanoscale coupling relieves frictional stress via multiple deformation pathways. At elevated temperatures (up to 800 °C), the nanoprecipitates help to trigger the formation of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate—potentially by an order of magnitude—compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi across the full temperature range.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which shows challenges in maintaining low friction and wear performance at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is operative under sliding loads in ambient air, with the temperature boundary from room temperature (≈25 °C) to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the optimal concentration and specific choice of the additive element to reliably form stable nanoprecipitates and the reproducibility of the adaptive glaze layer formation at high temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set of base CoCrFeNi alloy and a second set with a minor addition (e.g., 2-5 atomic %) of titanium to induce nanoprecipitate formation. Process both sets under identical conditions. Subject the samples to sliding tests in ambient air with controlled load and sliding speed at room temperature and at 800 °C. Characterize the microstructure using TEM/SEM to detect the presence of nanoprecipitates and the formation of a nanocrystalline glaze layer.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding at both RT and 800 °C
Microstructural analysis (grain size, distribution of nanoprecipitates, and surface layer characterization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with the additive does not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi across the temperature range, and if microstructural characterization fails to reveal the formation of a nanohierarchical structure with adaptive glaze layer at high temperature, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
